Cetaceans are widely regarded as indicator species; their spatial distribution and abundance are essential for understanding the ecosystem they live in. The waters around Gibraltar lie within a designated Important Marine Mammal Area (IMMA) at the Atlantic–Mediterranean boundary, yet no systematic assessment of cetacean distribution exists there. This study implements land-based distance sampling, a cost-effective, reproducible method adapted for fixed observation stations, in order to estimate the species composition, spatial distribution, density, and abundance of cetaceans around Gibraltar. A total of 174 standardised 10-minute watches were completed, corresponding to 27 hours of on-effort observation, during which 126 cetacean sightings were recorded. The highest density of common dolphins (*Delphinus delphis*) occurred in the southern sector, off the southern tip of the peninsula, at 4.66 individuals per km² (95% CI: 2.81–7.73), with an estimated 546 individuals within the surveyed area (95% CI: 329–906). Estimated density in the southern sector was 19 times higher than the eastern sector and 15 times higher than the western sector. This concentration of dolphins in a heavily trafficked area raises significant conservation and management concerns, particularly as the Mediterranean common dolphin is classified as Endangered under the IUCN Red List. Systematic survey revealed a markedly different spatial distribution from opportunistic records, which concentrated along the western side of Gibraltar and largely under-represented the eastern waters. These findings highlight the need for systematic assessments in this undersampled area and targeted protection and management measures in areas of high dolphin density.
